questions.q: Who were the two main leaders facing each other during the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
questions.a: The leaders were Robert Clive (for the Company) and Siraj-ud-Daulah (the Nawab of Bengal). A wrong answer suggests the student is mixing up historical figures, likely confusing them with later events like the 1857 Revolt.

questions.q: Was the Battle of Plassey won primarily because of the Company’s superior weapons and training?
questions.a: No, it was won through treachery, specifically the bribery of Mir Jafar. A "Yes" answer reveals the student missed the core lesson about how the Company gained power through manipulation rather than raw military might.

questions.q: If you were a historian, why would you say Mir Jafar’s decision to switch sides was the most important moment of the battle?
questions.a: Steps: 1. Acknowledge Mir Jafar was the Nawab's general. 2. Note he held a large portion of the army. 3. Observe that his betrayal left the Nawab unprotected. 4. Conclude the battle's outcome was decided by this choice. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks battles are only about who has more soldiers.

questions.q: How did the victory at Plassey change the status of the East India Company in India?
questions.a: It changed them from a purely trading group into a political power that could install its own choice of ruler. A wrong answer shows a failure to grasp the transition from "business" to "government."

questions.q: Is it fair to call the victory at Plassey a "military" victory in the traditional sense?
questions.a: No, because a traditional military victory implies a fair fight of skill and strength, whereas this was a result of political betrayal. Justifying this shows the student understands the difference between a skirmish and a political takeover. A wrong answer indicates the student equates "winning a battle" only with "killing the enemy."

questions.q: If the Company had not bribed Mir Jafar, what do you think might have happened to their influence in Bengal?
questions.a: They likely would have remained simple traders, as they lacked the force to defeat the Nawab's army alone. A poor answer ignores the power gap between the small Company force and the vast Bengal army.
